instagram_caption:
🚨 From breakout to blowup: how telehealth went from niche startup to Wall Street mania — and then reality hit.

In 2015 Teladoc debuted publicly with a market cap near $2B. By 2020, as COVID-19 forced clinics to close and patients went virtual, Teladoc rocketed to the spotlight — we show a leap from $9.5B in 2019 to $14.0B in 2020 and then a peak of $38.0B in 2021. Amwell shows a similar, shorter spike: effectively zero in public markets through 2019, jumping to $4.8B in 2020 and another surge into 2021.

But the story isn’t just fireworks. The chart race captures the crash: Teladoc collapses to $12B in 2022 and down to $1.8B by 2023 in market-cap terms, while Amwell tumbles under $1B. Those brutal reversals reflect churn: unprofitable growth, integrations (Livongo), and investor reassessment of unit economics once in-person care regained footing.

Contrast that with the incumbents. UnitedHealth climbs steadily from ~$35B in 2006 to a juggernaut — $480B in 2024 — as it broadened services, M&A and pushed into tech-enabled care. CVS shows a different path: steady retail and health services value, spikes around major deals, and a market-cap stabilization as it integrated pharmacy and care delivery.

What this visualization reveals is a classic market-cycle: pure-play telehealth companies exploded during a demand shock, then faced execution and profitability realities. Incumbents kept growing more quietly by acquiring capabilities and embedding virtual care into larger ecosystems.
